title: Privacy Policy
excerpt: How GE CHEMICAL & POLYMER GROUP CO., LTD handles information submitted through this website.
content:
Who we are

GE CHEMICAL & POLYMER GROUP CO., LTD operates this B2B masterbatch website. This policy explains what happens to personal information connected with product, quotation and technical document inquiries.

What this policy covers

This policy covers information you choose to provide through the website and information created when you contact the team about an inquiry. It does not cover third-party websites reached through external links.

Information you may provide

An inquiry may ask for your name, company, email address, country or region, product interest, application, resin, processing method, target requirement, known product grade, quantity, destination port, requested documents and a message.

Provide only the information needed to review your request. Do not send confidential formulas, customer records or other sensitive material unless the team has asked for it through an appropriate business channel.

How the inquiry form works

When you submit the inquiry form, the details are stored in a private WordPress inquiry record that can be viewed by the internal review team. Where email delivery is configured, the team may also receive a notification email. The record is not publicly displayed.

Submitting the form does not approve a product, price, quantity, sample, delivery date or document request. The team reviews the information and replies by email.

How inquiry information is used

When you contact the team, information you provide may be used to understand the product or application, check the exact grade and document scope, prepare a response and maintain related business records. It may also be used to protect the website and prevent misuse.

When information may be shared

Information may be handled by service providers that host the website, deliver email or support security and maintenance. They are expected to process it only for those services.

Information may also be disclosed when required by law or when needed to protect legal rights. We do not sell personal information.

How long information is kept

Inquiry information is kept only as long as needed for the purpose for which it was provided and for related business or legal records. When it is no longer needed, it is deleted or anonymized.

Your choices

Depending on applicable law, you may ask for access to your personal information, correction, deletion, restriction or an objection to certain processing.

Contact the GE Chemical team through the business channel you already use for the inquiry and mark the message "Privacy request". The team may need to verify the request before responding.

Cookies and technical logs

The WordPress site may use essential cookies for administration, security and user preferences.

If Google Analytics 4 is enabled, Google may process analytics data such as page visits, referral source, device and browser information, approximate location and form conversion events. The event data used for inquiry reporting does not include the submitted name, company, email address, message or other form contents. Google Analytics is not used by this site for advertising personalization.

If Meta Pixel and the Meta Conversions API are enabled, Meta (Facebook and Instagram) may receive page view and form conversion events from this website to measure advertising performance. The server-side conversion request includes a hashed version of the submitted email address (SHA-256), the visitor IP address and browser details, but not the submitted name, company, message or other form contents. Browser and server events share one event identifier so Meta can count each conversion once.

The web server and hosting infrastructure may record standard technical information such as IP address, browser details, requested page and time of access. These logs are used for security, troubleshooting and service reliability.

Children

This is a business website and is not directed to children. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children.

Changes to this policy

This policy may be updated when website forms, service providers or data practices change. The latest version will remain available at /privacy-policy/ with a revised update date.

Contact

For a question about this policy or your information, contact the GE Chemical team through the business channel used for your inquiry and mark the message "Privacy request".

title: Request Masterbatch Technical Documents
excerpt: Request review of technical or compliance-related documents for a specific black or desiccant masterbatch inquiry. Availability is checked by grade, application, country and intended use.
content:
GE CHEMICAL & POLYMER GROUP CO., LTD reviews each request by product interest, product grade, application, country or region and document scope before replying by email.

When buyers need document review

Technical documents may be needed for internal evaluation, customer approval, import review, compliance discussion or sample testing. The same document type does not necessarily apply to every product or grade.

Common request situations include:

  • A distributor needs documents for customer review.
  • A packaging or plastic product factory needs technical data before sample discussion.
  • A buyer needs SDS/MSDS or COA information for internal evaluation.
  • A customer asks whether RoHS-related, FDA-related or food-contact-related documents can be reviewed for a specific inquiry.

Information to prepare before requesting documents

  • Product interest: black masterbatch, desiccant masterbatch or not sure.
  • Product grade or model, if known.
  • Application or final plastic product.
  • Base resin, such as PE, PP, LDPE, LLDPE, HDPE, ABS, PET, PVC or another resin.
  • Processing method, such as film blowing, injection molding, extrusion or re-granulating.
  • Country or region where the product or document will be used.
  • Required document type.
  • Document purpose, such as internal evaluation, customer approval, import clearance, compliance review or sample testing.
  • Current grade, previous supplier grade or customer standard that should be reviewed.

How document requests are handled

Documents are requested by form and reviewed manually. This website does not publish or automatically deliver technical files after submission.

The review considers:

  • Product interest.
  • Product grade or model, if known.
  • Application.
  • Base resin and processing method.
  • Country or region.
  • Requested document type.
  • Intended use of the document.

If suitable documents are available, the team replies by email after review.

Compliance-related document boundaries

Compliance-related documents, if available, apply only to specific tested grades or samples. A request for an FDA-related, food-contact-related or RoHS-related document does not imply that every product or grade is covered.

Not every product has every document. Public page copy cannot confirm document availability before the exact grade and application are reviewed.

Before you submit

Share the exact product direction and application context you have. If the grade is unknown, provide the resin, process, final product, country and document purpose so the team can identify the right review path.

The form below asks for the required document type and purpose. Submitting a request does not approve a product, price, quantity, sample, delivery date or document request.

title: Masterbatch RFQ Checklist
excerpt: A complete inquiry gives the team enough context to review product fit and document scope without guessing the application.
content:
Use this checklist to prepare the information a masterbatch supplier usually needs before product and document review.

Product and application

  • Product direction: black, desiccant or not sure.
  • Final product or application.
  • Current issue or improvement target.
  • Application environment or customer requirement, where relevant.

Resin and process

  • Base resin, such as PE, PP, LDPE, LLDPE, HDPE, ABS, PET or PVC.
  • Processing method, such as film blowing, injection molding, extrusion or re-granulating.
  • Current grade or supplier, if known.
  • Existing addition ratio for the current product, if known.

Target requirement

  • Blackness, appearance or moisture-control target.
  • Dispersion, appearance or processing concern.
  • Tolerance expectation, if the buyer has one.

Quantity and destination

  • Trial quantity.
  • Estimated monthly quantity.
  • Destination country or region.
  • Destination port.

Documents

  • Required document type: TDS, SDS/MSDS, COA or a compliance-related request.
  • Intended use of the document.
  • Exact grade or current product, if known.

Document availability depends on the exact product grade, application, country and review. Compliance-related documents, if available, apply only to specific tested grades or samples.

Send the inquiry

Use the Request a Quote form for product review or the Technical Documents form for document review. You can select black or desiccant masterbatch in either form.

The more complete the information is, the easier it is for the team to identify what must be checked before any product, sample or document response.

title: How to Choose Masterbatch for Blown Film
excerpt: Use resin, carrier, film structure, thickness, let-down ratio and trial conditions to select masterbatch for blown film.
content:
Blown film makes some material problems easy to see. A particle, streak or color variation that stays hidden inside a thick molded part can appear across a thin film within seconds. That visibility helps quality control, but it also makes film masterbatch selection less forgiving.

The useful question is not simply "which grade is for film?" Film is a process and a family of products. A shopping bag, agricultural film, lamination layer and co-extruded barrier structure may all be blown, yet they can place different demands on resin, carrier, blackness, dispersion and documents.

This guide sets out the information a buyer should gather before asking for a grade, the questions to put to a supplier, and the trial conditions that make a result comparable.

Define the film before choosing the masterbatch

A supplier needs five points before it can review a film masterbatch direction:

  • Base resin and grade
  • Monolayer or co-extruded structure
  • Layer where the masterbatch will be used
  • Film thickness and expected let-down ratio
  • Final application and required documents

Record the actual resin grade where possible. PE, LDPE, LLDPE and PP are useful families, but they do not describe every polymer grade in the plant. Two PE resins can differ in melt behavior, density and processing window. The masterbatch carrier has to be considered against the resin actually used.

For a co-extruded film, state which layer carries the masterbatch. A skin layer, core layer and tie layer serve different functions. A product that works in one layer or structure is not automatically suitable for another.

Film thickness affects how visible a defect becomes and how much blackness or opacity must be delivered from the added masterbatch. The application determines whether the priority is blackness, dispersion, barrier support, surface behavior or moisture control. It also determines which technical documents may be needed.

The masterbatch RFQ checklist can be used to collect these inputs in one format.

Check carrier compatibility

Masterbatch is a concentrate carried into the melt by a carrier resin and other components. The carrier must melt and mix within the process window of the base resin. A PE carrier is a starting direction for a PE film, not proof that every PE grade has been checked.

Ask the supplier:

  • What carrier does the grade use?
  • Has the carrier been reviewed for this resin family and film process?
  • Does the supplier expect any difference in mixing, feeding or surface behavior?
  • If the resin changes, which part of the previous trial remains relevant?

The last question matters during sourcing changes. A trial result belongs to the identified resin, masterbatch, machine and conditions. If one of those changes, the buyer should review whether a new trial or supplier confirmation is needed.

Select black masterbatch by film criteria

Black masterbatch for blown film is judged by blackness, dispersion, carrier compatibility and the way the grade behaves on the actual line.

Black film is often judged by blackness and consistency, yet dispersion can matter more than the headline carbon black percentage. Carbon black is a fine pigment, and poorly dispersed agglomerates can appear as specks or streaks in thin film.

Ask for the carrier resin, carbon black loading, intended addition range and dispersion controls. Request the current TDS for the exact grade. Where a trial is proposed, define the target blackness, film thickness and addition ratio before running it.

A high carbon black percentage may support a lower addition ratio, but the buyer should compare cost in use and dispersion rather than the percentage alone. The black masterbatch guide explains the relationship between loading, filler and grade position.

Review the let-down ratio as a system variable

The let-down ratio is the amount of masterbatch added to the base resin. It influences blackness, opacity, dispersion demand and cost. It also changes how much carrier enters the final formulation.

For each proposed grade, ask:

  • What addition ratio did the supplier use to develop or describe the product?
  • Is that a starting recommendation, a typical production range or a customer-specific value?
  • What feeding method was used?
  • Did the supplier assess the final film at the planned ratio?

Compare cost in use where possible. Calculate the cost of masterbatch required for a defined production quantity, then check whether the trial result was obtained at that ratio. A lower price per kilogram with a higher use rate may not reduce cost.

The current TDS is the starting document for grade-specific values. Any addition range should remain tied to the exact product and should be confirmed in the trial.

Check processing conditions and line response

Blown film trials can expose problems that a datasheet does not describe: unstable bubbles, die build-up, gels, specks, surface defects, excessive pressure or inconsistent blackness. Ask the supplier which processing conditions matter for the grade and how those conditions were assessed.

Record the actual line conditions used in the trial:

  • Extruder zones and melt temperature
  • Screw speed and output
  • Die and air conditions
  • Frost line and film thickness
  • Screen pack or filtration setup
  • Feeding method and addition ratio
  • Start-up, purge and changeover steps

A supplier does not need to guarantee every machine setting. It should be able to explain which conditions affect the product and which observations would require follow-up.

Use a trial with agreed conditions

A sample trial is more useful when both parties agree on what will be compared. Before the material arrives, record:

A successful trial supports one result in one defined setup. It does not automatically prove every future batch, another line or another film structure. Ask separately how the supplier controls batch consistency and what records accompany production.

Read the TDS with the film application in view

A TDS can identify the product, carrier, typical properties, test methods and intended scope. It does not replace a film trial.

Check the document version and grade first. Then read each value with its method and condition. Confirm whether the number is typical, specified or an acceptance value. For blackness, opacity, melt flow, moisture and dispersion-related properties, the method and conditions determine whether the values are comparable.

If the film requires a technical or compliance document, ask for the exact scope. A TDS, SDS, COA, test report and declaration answer different questions. Use the technical document request process when document availability and applicability still need review.

Questions to send a supplier

This set is short enough for a first technical exchange:

  1. Which grade do you recommend for this resin, film structure, thickness and application?
  2. What carrier does the grade use?
  3. What is the intended addition ratio, and what basis supports it?
  4. Which properties should be checked before the trial?
  5. Which current TDS applies to the exact grade?
  6. Can you provide a sample with a grade and batch or date reference?
  7. What trial conditions should we agree before running the sample?
  8. Which documents apply to the target market and end use?
  9. How do you control and report batch consistency?
  10. What changes would require a new sample review?

When a supplier answers with assumptions and missing inputs rather than a universal promise, that is useful information. It shows where the review must continue.

A film masterbatch selection record

Keep the review in one place so another person can follow it.

Continue with the right technical question

Film selection becomes easier when the buyer separates product category, application and evidence. Start with the masterbatch direction that matches the material and film requirement, then use the exact grade, current documents and a controlled trial to decide whether it belongs in production.

If black specks, streaks or uneven dispersion appear during a trial, use the black specks diagnostic guide to collect evidence before assigning a cause. Product inquiries can be submitted through the request a quote form.

title: Poor Dispersion and Black Specks in Masterbatch Film: A Diagnostic Guide
excerpt: Collect a control sample and production records, compare possible material and process directions, and verify the defect with a controlled trial.
content:
Black specks, dark streaks and uneven color in plastic film can come from several parts of the process. The visible defect identifies where to begin looking. It does not identify the cause.

A batch of masterbatch may be involved. So might the base resin, feeding setup, machine condition, purge procedure, screen pack, temperature profile, contamination source or observation method. Starting with one cause before collecting a comparison sample often turns a solvable quality issue into an argument.

This guide gives buyers, processors and suppliers one sequence for collecting useful evidence and deciding the next test.

Describe the defect before discussing responsibility

Use observable language. "Black specks about 0.3 mm wide, concentrated near the bubble edge, present continuously in the current run" gives more information than "the masterbatch is bad."

Record:

  • Defect type: speck, gel, particle, streak, color patch or other visible pattern
  • Size and approximate frequency
  • Position in the film, across the bubble or in a particular layer
  • Whether the defect appears on the surface, inside the film or throughout the structure
  • When it started and which run or batch was involved
  • Whether it appears continuously, intermittently or only at start-up
  • Whether the film thickness or machine settings changed
  • Which products and batches were present when the defect appeared

A photograph helps, but it should not be the only evidence. Include the full film or roll in at least one view, then take closer views with a scale or reference object. Record lighting and camera distance so another person can interpret the image.

The Buyer FAQ provides general answers about samples and document review, but a quality investigation should use the actual batch and process records.

Secure a control sample

A control sample gives the defect a comparison point. It should come from a run that met the agreed quality requirement and should have enough production information to make the comparison meaningful.

Record the control sample's:

  • Masterbatch grade and batch
  • Base resin grade and batch
  • Film structure and thickness
  • Addition ratio and feeding method
  • Machine and main processing conditions
  • Production date
  • Inspection result or acceptance record

If no control sample exists, collect the closest available good production sample and state what is unknown. A comparison with an unidentified sample can still help, but it should not be treated as a controlled test.

Collect the evidence pack

A useful first evidence pack contains six groups.

Keep the problem and control samples labelled. A sample without a product reference, batch, date and source becomes difficult to use after a few days.

Check five possible directions

The evidence pack supports a structured review. It does not create a hierarchy of blame.

Material

Check whether the masterbatch, resin or another raw material changed. Record batch references, storage conditions, drying records and any substitution or re-sourcing.

Ask for the TDS for the grade in use and the COA or inspection record for the affected batch where available. A current document describes or reports a defined product scope. It does not, by itself, explain a visible defect.

Addition and feeding

Confirm the addition ratio that was planned and the ratio actually delivered to the melt. Review calibration, feeder stability, pre-mixing, separate feeding, reclaim addition and refill practice.

A change in apparent color or dispersion may follow a change in effective addition. The feeding records should be compared with the control run rather than assumed.

Process

Compare temperature, output, speed, pressure, bubble stability and filtration records. Look for changes around the first appearance of the defect.

A single temperature reading may not describe the heat history of the material. Barrel residence time, shutdowns, low-output periods and start-up conditions can also matter. Record what is available.

Equipment

Review the screw, barrel, die, screen pack and material path. Check maintenance, purge, color-change and cleaning records. A machine that is mechanically different from the control run may produce a different visible result.

Filtration evidence should be treated as one clue. A pressure rise or screen blockage shows that material is being captured. It does not establish what the material is or where it entered the process.

Environment and handling

Check material storage, open containers, dust controls, cleaning, regrind handling and handover between shifts. A contamination event may leave no record in the masterbatch batch file.

Use a comparison sequence

1. Confirm that the defect is repeatable

Inspect more than one section of the affected run. A single speck can be a local event. A pattern that repeats under the same conditions provides a stronger basis for a controlled test.

2. Compare with the control run

Place the problem film and control film side by side. Use the same lighting and observation distance. Look for differences in speck frequency, streak direction, color and position through the film.

3. List what changed

Build a simple comparison:

An empty cell is useful. It identifies the evidence that still needs to be collected.

4. Change one variable at a time

Where production allows, run a controlled comparison with the same resin, machine, addition ratio and conditions. Change one recorded variable, such as the masterbatch batch, then compare the result.

If several variables change at once, the test may reveal an improvement or deterioration, but it will not identify which change produced the result.

5. Record the result

Record:

  • Materials and batch references
  • Machine and conditions
  • Change introduced
  • Samples collected
  • Observation or test result
  • Person who approved the conclusion

The conclusion should stay within the test scope. A result from one line, product and batch does not automatically cover another.

Separate defect types

Different visible patterns need different records. The names below describe appearance. They do not establish a source.

Black specks

Record size, count, shape, distribution and whether the speck sits on the surface or inside the film. Retain the problem film and the raw materials used in the run.

Dark streaks

Record direction, width, location across the bubble and whether the streak continues through the roll. Note layer position in a co-extruded film and any die or flow-path work.

Gels or unmelted particles

Record shape and whether the particle deforms under heat or pressure. Compare with the control film and inspect the resin and masterbatch records. A visual particle identification may need laboratory support.

Uneven color

Record the color reference, measured result where available, addition ratio, resin and film thickness. Do not assign the difference to dispersion before checking the comparison conditions.

Surface deposits or die build-up

Record where the deposit forms, when it starts and what material remains after cleaning. Include purge and shutdown records because the material history may differ from steady-state production.

Customer complaint intake

When a customer reports a film defect, the first reply should obtain enough evidence to schedule the right review.

Ask in phases. A first message can request the problem sample, control sample, product references and approximate production date. Detailed machine records can follow once the samples show that a technical review is needed.

What a supplier response should show

A useful supplier response identifies what is known, what is missing and what can be tested. It does not immediately name a cause or deny responsibility.

A weak response:

Our masterbatch cannot cause black specks. The problem is in your machine.

A more useful response:

We need the affected film, a control film, the masterbatch and resin batch references, the addition ratio and the main process records. The cause is not yet confirmed. We can compare the masterbatch batch against the retained sample and arrange a controlled trial after reviewing the feeding and screen-pack history.

The second response creates a path to evidence. It still leaves the cause open.

A first technical reply template

We have received the report of [defect] from [production date or roll reference]. At this stage the cause is not confirmed.

To review it, please provide:

• Problem film and a control film
• Masterbatch and resin grades and batch references
• Film structure and thickness
• Addition ratio and feeder records
• Main temperature, output and pressure records
• Screen-pack, purge and maintenance history
• Photographs showing the defect and its position

After the samples and records are reviewed, we will propose the next comparison or trial. The scope of that trial will be agreed before it starts.

Prevent the next unclear investigation

Most complaint delays begin before the defect. Production records are incomplete, samples are not labelled, or the masterbatch batch cannot be linked to the roll.

The following controls make future reviews easier:

  • Record masterbatch and resin batches at start-up and at material changes
  • Keep a retention sample for each masterbatch lot as agreed with the supplier
  • Record the actual addition ratio and feeder calibration
  • Keep start-up, purge and shutdown records
  • Label problem samples with machine, product, date and roll
  • Keep a control sample from an approved run
  • Record process changes against the production date
  • Define who will approve a return to normal production

These controls do not prevent every defect. They make the cause easier to test when a defect appears.

Continue with a controlled comparison

Start with the sample and records, then choose the test. For film selection or supplier questions, use the blown-film masterbatch selection guide. For a material direction, review black masterbatch. If technical files are needed, use the technical document request process and keep the request tied to the exact grade, batch and end use.

title: How to Vet a Masterbatch Supplier: A Practical Buyer Checklist
excerpt: Use one supplier review to check the legal entity, technical documents, sample trial, batch controls, quotation basis and change process.
content:
Most supplier comparisons begin with a price. That is too early. Before comparing prices, a buyer needs to establish what each supplier is actually offering, which legal entity is responsible, what the technical documents cover, and whether the quoted grade can be checked on the buyer's own resin and process.

A useful supplier review does not prove that every future batch will perform in the same way. It shows whether the supplier can answer specific questions, provide traceable records, and define the limits of its own claims. That is the standard this checklist uses.

Define the purchase before you judge the supplier

A supplier cannot give a comparable answer if the inquiry only says "need black masterbatch" or "send your best price". Prepare the same product brief for every supplier:

  • Base resin and grade, if known
  • Processing method and the most relevant operating conditions
  • Final product, structure, dimensions or wall thickness where relevant
  • Color, appearance or functional target
  • Current problem, if one exists
  • Current grade or supplier, if the material is being replaced
  • Trial quantity and expected monthly volume
  • Target market and required documents
  • Packaging, destination and required delivery date, if already known

The masterbatch RFQ checklist explains these inputs in more detail. Sending a consistent brief makes supplier replies easier to compare and makes vague answers easier to spot.

Verify who you are buying from

The company on the website is not always the company that will issue the quotation, invoice or technical document. Ask for the legal entity name, registered address and the role the company will play in the order.

A supplier may be a manufacturer, a converter, an exporter or a trading company. Any of these roles can work, but the responsibility must be clear. If a trading company supplies the material, ask who makes it and whose TDS, COA and complaint records will support the order.

Check that these names remain consistent:

  • Quotation and sales contract
  • Proforma invoice and commercial invoice
  • Bank beneficiary
  • TDS, SDS and COA issuer
  • Packaging and shipping marks
  • Company address and contact details

Ask for the scope of any management-system certificate. An ISO 9001 certificate, for example, supports a quality-management claim for the activities and sites named in the certificate. It does not establish that a particular masterbatch grade meets the buyer's color, processing or regulatory requirement.

A live video review or site visit can help confirm that the reported address, equipment and material handling match the company's description. Where travel is not practical, ask for a short live walk-through rather than relying only on edited photographs.

Read the documents by scope

The value of a technical document comes from the product, grade, batch or test it covers. A document with no clear scope cannot support a broad supplier claim.

Three distinctions prevent most document mistakes.

First, a TDS is not a batch certificate. A typical value describes the product in general terms. A specification states a requirement the supplier expects to meet. An acceptance value belongs to an agreement between buyer and supplier. Ask which type of value appears in the document.

Second, a COA covers one batch unless the document clearly says otherwise. Ask for the COA or inspection record tied to the material being offered, not an undated example passed around as a quality brochure.

Third, a compliance document is limited to the grade, sample, standard and test shown in it. A RoHS report for one black sample does not cover every black grade. An FDA-related report for one white sample does not make the full white range suitable for food contact. Use the technical document request process when the exact grade and intended use still need review.

Test whether the numbers are usable

A number without a method and condition can create false confidence. The same property measured under different conditions may not be directly comparable.

For melt flow rate or melt volume flow rate, ask whether the result is MFR or MVR, the temperature and load used, the unit, and whether the document reports a typical value or a specification. A melt-flow result supports quality control. It does not prove how the material will run on a particular machine.

For color difference, the numeric result depends on the reference sample, base resin, masterbatch addition ratio, sample preparation, instrument, illuminant and measurement conditions. A delta E value without those details is not enough for supplier comparison.

For pigment or filler content, ask what the percentage refers to and whether it is measured, calculated or stated as a nominal formulation value. Carbon black loading and CaCO3 filler can change blackness, opacity, gloss, density and cost. They should be compared only with the grade and test basis in view.

Judge how the supplier handles your application

A supplier that understands masterbatch should ask questions before recommending a grade. Useful questions include:

  • What resin is the product made from?
  • Is the process blown film, injection molding, extrusion, blow molding, spinning or another method?
  • What is the final product and which property matters most?
  • What is the current appearance or performance target?
  • Is there an existing grade, control sample or production problem?
  • What addition ratio is planned or currently used?
  • What documents are required for the target market and end use?

A supplier may not need every answer before the first reply. The useful signal is whether the supplier recognizes the missing information and explains what must be confirmed next. A recommendation that ignores resin, process and end use has little technical value.

Look for answers that separate facts from assumptions. A careful reply may say:

The TDS lists this grade for PE film. We still need the exact resin, film thickness and target opacity before confirming the trial direction.

That kind of response is easier to verify than "suitable for all films".

Compare cost with the full product basis

Two quotations are comparable only when they describe the same product and commercial basis. Before ranking price, confirm:

  • Grade and product version
  • Carrier resin
  • Pigment, filler or functional content where relevant
  • Packaging size and material
  • Quantity basis
  • Incoterm and destination
  • Currency
  • Quote validity
  • Expected lead time
  • Payment terms
  • Whether the price includes the required documents or tests

A cheaper price per kilogram may require a higher addition ratio. It may also include more filler, a different carrier, a smaller package or a less convenient delivery term. Compare expected cost against the finished product using the supplier's stated basis, then confirm that basis in a trial.

Review the sample and trial plan

Ask for a sample that carries a grade name, batch or date reference and handling information. A sample with no identity is difficult to compare with the production material later.

Before the trial, agree on:

  • Exact masterbatch grade and sample reference
  • Base resin and grade
  • Addition ratio and feeding method
  • Machine and main processing conditions
  • Product or film structure, thickness or wall section
  • Control sample for comparison
  • Properties to inspect
  • Pass or follow-up criteria
  • Who will record the result

A trial can show that one identified sample ran in a defined setup. It does not establish batch-to-batch consistency by itself. Ask how the next production batch will be checked and which records will be supplied with it.

The Buyer FAQ covers related questions about trial samples and document review.

Check batch control and complaint handling

An acceptable first sample is useful. A supplier also needs a repeatable way to tell the buyer when something changes.

Ask how the supplier:

  • Identifies production batches
  • Keeps retained samples
  • Records inspection results
  • Handles a change in raw material, formulation or process
  • Notifies customers when a change may affect the product
  • Investigates color, dispersion, contamination or processing complaints

When a quality issue appears, a useful supplier asks for the problem sample, control sample, batch references, resin, addition ratio, processing records and a clear description of the defect before assigning a cause. "Not our problem" is not an investigation.

The supplier should also explain what its COA covers. A COA that reports only one property may be valid for that property and insufficient for another requirement. Ask for the methods and results that match the decision you need to make.

Put the commercial terms under change control

Product and commercial assumptions change together. A new resin, target color, packaging format, destination or monthly quantity can alter the grade, document requirement or quotation.

Create a short change record whenever one of these items changes:

The record does not need to be complicated. It needs to prevent an old sample, COA or quotation from being treated as valid after the conditions have changed.

A 45-minute desk review

Use this sequence before moving a supplier to the sample stage.

Minutes 0 to 10: identity

Confirm the legal entity, address, role in the supply chain and consistency between quotation, invoice and bank details. Ask who issues the TDS and COA.

Minutes 10 to 20: product definition

Check that the supplier can identify the exact grade, carrier, intended process and main product properties. Mark any claim that uses only vague category language.

Minutes 20 to 30: document scope

Request the TDS and a COA example for the offered grade. For any compliance claim, ask for the grade, sample, standard, test date and intended scope. Make a list of what is still missing.

Minutes 30 to 40: technical response

Send the same application brief used for other suppliers. Compare whether the reply addresses resin, process, end use, target and documents, or jumps directly to a price.

Minutes 40 to 45: next step

Decide whether the supplier should receive a sample request, provide more documents or remain on hold. Record the reason. Do not move forward only because the sales response was fast.

Warning signs

Treat these as questions for further review:

  • The quotation, invoice, bank beneficiary and document issuer use unrelated company names.
  • The supplier sends a TDS for a different grade.
  • The supplier says all products meet every certification without giving a grade or test scope.
  • A COA has no batch reference or test method.
  • A technical value has no unit, condition or indication of whether it is typical or specified.
  • The supplier promises suitability without asking about resin, process or end use.
  • The supplier cannot explain how a batch change is communicated.
  • A complaint is answered with blame before any evidence is collected.
  • The quoted material cannot be tied to a sample or production batch reference.

None of these points automatically ends a supplier review. Each one creates a follow-up question and a record of what remains unverified.

A short supplier review email

This message can be sent after the first product discussion. Adjust the fields to the actual application.

Subject: Technical and document review for [product / grade]

Hello [name],

Before we compare the quotation, please confirm the following:

1. Legal entity name, production site and your role in the supply chain
2. Exact grade and carrier resin being quoted
3. TDS version and date
4. Which TDS values are typical and which are specifications
5. COA example for the offered grade, with batch reference and test methods
6. SDS version for the product being supplied
7. Any compliance document, including the grade or sample, standard, test date and scope
8. Recommended sample quantity and trial conditions for [resin, process and application]
9. Packaging, quantity basis, Incoterm, destination, currency and quote validity
10. How you notify customers about changes that may affect product performance

Our application brief is attached. Please identify any information we still need to provide.

Regards,
[buyer]

Supplier review record

Use one row per supplier so the comparison remains visible.

What a good answer looks like

A good supplier answer is specific enough to check. It names the grade, document, batch or test being discussed. It states assumptions. It says when a question needs the buyer's resin, process or end use before an answer can be given.

That standard applies to every supplier. Product pages can help shortlist a material direction, but they do not replace the supplier review. Use the Black masterbatch or Desiccant masterbatch page to identify the relevant product function, then ask each supplier to support its offer with documents and a trial plan.

For a new inquiry, start with the request a quote form or review technical documents when the file scope is the main question.

For the material side of the review, use the film masterbatch selection guide. If a trial produces black specks or streaks, use the diagnostic guide to collect comparable evidence.

title: How to Choose Carbon Black Content in Black Masterbatch
excerpt: Use resin, filler, dispersion, let-down ratio and a line trial to choose the right carbon black content for black masterbatch.
content:
The carbon black percentage on a masterbatch TDS is useful, but it does not choose the grade for you. A 40% product can deliver more pigment per kilogram than a 20% product. It can also cost more, feed differently, require a different let-down ratio and change the surface of the finished part.

The right starting point is the final product and the process that will make it. Buyers then compare the carbon black content with the carrier, filler, dispersion, target blackness and cost in use. This guide explains that comparison and the evidence needed before a grade is approved for production.

What carbon black content in black masterbatch means

Carbon black content is the share of carbon black in the masterbatch pellet. It is not the carbon black content of the finished plastic part. The let-down ratio determines how much masterbatch enters the final formulation.

For example, 4 kg of a 30% grade added to 100 kg of compound contains about 1.2 kg of carbon black, before losses. The same addition rate with a 40% grade contains about 1.6 kg. The higher-loading grade can supply more pigment at the same feed setting, but that arithmetic does not yet prove that it will disperse well or meet the appearance target.

The percentage also does not identify the carbon black itself. Carbon black grades can differ in particle size, structure and surface treatment. Those differences can affect tone, color development and the amount of work needed to disperse the pigment. Two products with the same headline percentage can therefore behave differently in the same resin and process.

Read carbon black, carrier and filler as one system

A black masterbatch contains more than carbon black. The current TDS examples for BK020 to BK040 list carbon black, an LLDPE and LDPE carrier, a dispersion agent and CaCO3 filler. Their shares change together.

These values belong to the listed TDS examples. Ask for the current TDS for the grade being offered and check that the grade, revision and values have not changed.

Across this range, carbon black rises from 20% to 40% while the listed CaCO3 filler falls from 47.8% to 5.8%. A lower-loading product can therefore contain much more filler. A higher-loading product can deliver more carbon black and less filler per kilogram, subject to its actual formulation.

The carrier is the second part of the comparison. The current BK examples use the same resin family, but the carrier share is not the same in every grade. A buyer still needs to confirm the carrier against the actual base resin, processing temperature and final product. A familiar abbreviation such as PE or PP is not enough to approve compatibility.

How the 20% to 40% range changes

Loading bands are a way to narrow the trial, not a universal grade chart. A 20% grade from one supplier is not interchangeable with a 20% grade from another supplier if the carbon black, carrier, filler or dispersion changes.

Lower loadings around 20% to 25%

Lower-loading grades leave more room for filler in the examples above. They can be a practical starting direction when the final product is thick enough to carry more filler and the appearance target is less demanding. Trash bags, general molded parts and re-granulating are application directions listed in the current BK TDS examples.

The lower pigment share normally requires more masterbatch to deliver a target amount of carbon black. Buyers should check whether the lower compound price offsets the higher use rate. They should also check gloss, mechanical requirements and surface appearance if filler content matters to the product.

The middle of the range around 30%

A 30% grade can offer a useful balance between pigment load, carrier, filler and feed rate. It is often a reasonable grade to test when the application is known but the final loading has not been fixed.

That does not make 30% a default answer for every product. A thin film may need a different dispersion or surface result. A high-gloss molded part may need a lower filler level. A cost-sensitive thick section may work with less carbon black and more filler. The trial still decides.

Higher loadings around 35% to 40%

Higher-loading grades can deliver more pigment with less masterbatch. The BK040 example contains 40% carbon black and 5.8% CaCO3 filler. That combination can be relevant when the buyer needs a deep black, a cleaner high-gloss surface or a lower feed rate.

The trade-off is not limited to price per kilogram. A concentrated grade still has to feed consistently, melt with the base resin and disperse at the final addition ratio. A high percentage that creates specks, streaks or feeding variation has not solved the buyer's problem.

Why blackness alone does not settle the grade

Blackness describes the result the buyer wants to see or measure. It does not describe the full formulation that produces that result. The final appearance depends on the carbon black, pigment load, dispersion, carrier, filler, part thickness, surface finish and viewing or measurement method.

Thin film makes dispersion defects easy to see. An undispersed particle can appear as a speck or streak even when the TDS lists a high carbon black content. A molded part may hide small specks but make surface haze, flow lines or gloss differences more obvious.

Define blackness with a physical reference where possible. A retained sample, an approved production part or a measured color target is more useful than a description such as "very black". State the resin, masterbatch addition ratio, sample preparation and measurement conditions used for a numeric color result. A color number without those details is difficult to compare.

Calculate cost from the use rate

Price per kilogram is only one input. The useful comparison is the material cost required to make a defined quantity of acceptable product.

Masterbatch price per kg x let-down ratio x 1,000 = material cost per tonne

Use 0.05 for a 5% let-down ratio and 0.03 for a 3% ratio.

For illustration only, a USD 4.00 grade used at 5% gives USD 200 of masterbatch per tonne. A USD 6.00 grade used at 3% gives USD 180 per tonne. The higher-priced product may cost less to use, but only if the lower feed rate reaches the same appearance and runs reliably on the line.

The current BK TDS examples list a recommended addition ratio of 2% to 5%, with adjustment for actual production conditions. Treat that as a starting recommendation tied to the listed products, not a guarantee that every grade will meet the buyer's target inside that range.

Cost in use should also include the effects of failed parts, rejected film, line stops, feeding variation, purge time and any change in mechanical or surface properties. A quotation cannot settle those effects. A controlled trial and production record can.

Match the starting grade to the product and process

The following are trial directions, not automatic grade approvals:

  • Trash bags and general thick sections can begin with a lower or middle loading where filler is acceptable and the blackness target allows it.
  • Blown film should start with dispersion and surface quality. Test the exact resin, film structure, thickness and final let-down ratio. A higher-loading grade may reduce feed demand, but it still needs to run cleanly.
  • Injection molding may place more emphasis on color consistency, surface finish and flow. Compare the trial parts under the same lighting and measurement method.
  • Re-granulating and recycled feedstock can contain color variation. Black can mask some of that variation, but the required addition rate will depend on the feedstock and target appearance.

The black masterbatch guide explains the full product direction and document scope. Product pages should be used for grade-specific data, while this article provides the selection method.

Check the documents against the exact grade

A TDS is the first document for grade-specific values. Check the product name, revision, carbon black content, carrier, filler and recommended addition range. Ask which values are typical and which, if any, are acceptance limits.

An SDS covers handling, storage and transport information for the product and version stated in that document. A COA covers a specific production batch. A compliance report or declaration covers the exact grade, sample, standard and test named in it.

A statement such as "food grade" in a TDS does not by itself prove that the exact grade may be used in a food-contact application in the buyer's market. Ask for a current document that covers the grade, application, test method and regulatory scope required for the destination market.

Use the technical document request process when the required TDS, SDS, COA or compliance scope has not been confirmed for the exact grade.

Prepare a useful inquiry

An inquiry that says only "best price for black masterbatch" leaves every supplier to guess. Include:

  • Base resin and grade, if known
  • Process: blown film, injection molding, extrusion or another method
  • Final product, wall thickness or film structure where relevant
  • Appearance target and a physical or measured color reference
  • Current grade and addition ratio, if replacing an existing material
  • Trial quantity and expected monthly volume
  • Required documents and target market
  • Known processing limits or current production problem

The masterbatch RFQ checklist provides a consistent input list. A complete brief lets the supplier recommend a carbon black range without pretending that one grade fits every line.

Run a comparable trial

Keep the trial controlled. Record the base resin, masterbatch grade and batch, addition ratio, feeder setting, machine, temperature profile, output rate, film thickness or part dimensions, and inspection method.

Keep a control sample made under the same conditions without the candidate change, or use a recent approved production sample with enough records to make the comparison useful. Compare blackness, dispersion, surface, feeding stability and any mechanical requirement that matters to the product.

Run more than one addition ratio when the supplier's starting recommendation is wide. The result should show the lowest ratio that meets the agreed requirements and remains stable through a realistic production run. A single hand sample may show that a grade can make a black part. It does not prove that the grade is ready for an order.

Choose the grade after the evidence

There is no universal best carbon black content. A lower-loading grade may lower material cost when filler and appearance are acceptable. A higher-loading grade may reduce feed demand and support a cleaner surface when the line can disperse and feed it consistently.

Choose the grade that meets the product target at a stable addition ratio, with the carrier and documents reviewed for the actual application. Compare cost per tonne after the trial, not before it.

Review the black masterbatch range, request the current TDS and a sample for the shortlisted grade, or submit an inquiry with the resin, process and appearance target.
